newsitem.title: JAPAN: Activist from Hong Kong protest boat dies.
newsitem.headline: Activist from Hong Kong protest boat dies.

text.p: An activist from a Hong Kong vessel protesting Japan's claim to disputed islands in the East China Sea died on Thursday after jumping overboard, Japanese maritime officials said.
The death of group leader David Chan was the first in an increasingly bitter international dispute over the issue of whether Japan, Taiwan or China owns the desolate chain of uninhabited islands.
"A doctor from Japan who boarded the Hong Kong ship confirmed that Chan Yuk Cheung David was dead," a spokesman for Japan's Maritime Safety Agency told Reuters.
Officials said Chan and three other men jumped off the Hong Kong vessel, Kien Hwa 2, earlier in the day, although media reports from the scene said five men were involved.
One other man, Fong Yu Yuen, was injured and taken to hospital in southern Japan's Okinawa prefecture, where he was being kept on a respirator. The others were rescued unhurt.
The chartered vessel from Hong Kong had set sail for the islands on Sunday, and had twice entered what Japan considers its territorial waters.

The activists had vowed to reclaim the islands, known as the Senkakus in Japan and Diaoyus in Chinese, saying they would remove a lighthouse built by Japanese rightists in July and raise the red flag of the People's Republic of China.
The incident creates fresh headaches for the Japanese government, which had been trying to lower the temperature in the dispute.
Chan was declared dead when resuscitation efforts by coast guards from a nearby Japanese government ship failed.
The men dived from the ship when it was three miles (five km) from the islands, Hong Kong government radio said.

"They want to demonstrate to the Japanese that Chinese have the right to do whatever they want to do, including swimming in Chinese waters," its correspondent said. The activists were wearing lifejackets, the radio added.
The tanker was surrounded by 20 Japanese vessels, five planes and one helicopter, he said.
The incident follows a meeting between Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and his Japanese counterpart Yukihiko Ikeda in New York.

Qian asked that Japan take "concrete action" but Ikeda was noncommittal in his reply, urging China in turn to approach the situation reasonably and not let the issue interfere with the relations between the two countries.
